Enhancing the accuracy of ML algorithms is crucial, yet it requires a balanced approach that considers other aspects such as reliability. Our research focuses on the intersection of trustworthiness in ML and human interaction. We examine the issue of trust, exploring how to quantify it through metrics and examining what constitutes a trustworthy model. Consequently, we introduce a new notion termed "human supervision to increase reliability," which utilizes an interaction between humans and machines to address models where an increase in data leads to greater reliability. The human component involves agents evaluating the models' reliability on a scale from zero to one. The algorithm determines the optimal set of agent selections to maximize performance within the training set while requiring a limited number of contributions from agents to achieve results. Two distinct environments were utilized to validate the strategy in practice: a classification task using the MNIST image recognition set and a recommendation system based on Amazon products. Empirical results demonstrate that implementing this approach significantly addresses reliability with minimal manpower.

T2-weighted 3D MRI images are a standard for assessing most cancers, yet their clinical application is frequently hinderered by longer scan times. Extending the scan duration invites unwanted effects like reduced resolution due to motion and saturation from changing breathing states. While increasing the acceleration level has emerged as a primary solution to shorten scanning times—enhancing speed by an order of magnitude beyond previous limits—this often compromises image quality. Furthermore, while existing methods can compensate for different phases of breathing, few offer a robust solution for continuous free-breathing scans. To solve these challenges, we introduced a novel method utilizing sub-sampling in the depth of field (z-direction) to eliminate motion artifacts throughout the entire entire breathing cycle for T2-weighted 3D sequences. Testing on both real patient data and precise numerical simulations of respiratory movement demonstrated effective artifact removal without significant loss of overall image fidelity. Our technique outperformed that used for held-suspension breaths when evaluated against a full-breathing cycle in clinical settings and showed superiority over current reconstructed free-breathing methods in real patient T2 imaging.

Statistical testing for permutation statistics in cophenetic or correlation data is a pressing challenge in genealogical research, dendrology, and phylogeny. Although existing methods assess these statistics independently, they fail to account for the typical joint examination required in practice. We introduce the Precise Pair-Permutation Test (PPPT)—a precise technique that evaluates multiple tree structure metrics under permutation by approximating their full joint distribution. To do so, the model utilizes local search heuristics to analyze only near-permissible configurations, making it ideally suited for large-scale genetic datasets where sample sizes are considerable but computational capacities are limited regarding the number of possible permutations. We demonstrate through analysis that the PPPT achieves nearly optimal statistical inference even when sample sets extend beyond one thousand observations while processing standard structure indicators used in such studies.

Social interaction serves as a crucial learning mechanism, enabling the transmission not only of practical skills but also on a social awareness known as common ground. While prior research in offline settings has focused on teaching it via interactional dynamics that expert agents cannot utilize for task completion, such methods remain inapplicable in real time. To bridge the gap, we introduce Co-Observation Learning, a method trained solely on public data. This approach teaches modelled communication dynamics that are grounded in an shared information awareness, utilizing examples naturally available in raw datasets. We validated our approach in a diverse set of scenarios including conversation generation, legal advice chatbots and natural dialog systems to show that Co-Observation Learning succeeds at creating a modelled communication dynamics that are very realistic and effective in producing high quality interactions. Our results demonstrate that communication outputs generated by our model are significantly more realistic and meaningful, establishing a new state of the art communication outputs that are very high in quality.

This study examines advantage-based reinforcement learning applied to neural machine translation, addressing the challenge of selecting optimal neural network parameters using only human-labeled training data. A primary obstacle in off-line RL traditions is the high memory demand required to store an exhaustive set of trajectory data, rendering the approach unfeasible for models with vast action dimensions. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a projection-based algorithm that achieves an efficient solution without needing to retain training interactions. Additionally, within the specific context of neural translation, our work explores the selection of a suitable action distribution for integration into end-to-end translation models, and finally presents empirical results validating our method.

We present a theoretical framework analyzing the non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) of a Quantum Bit (NSS) in a periodically driven NSS, focusing on the case where the driving period is very long. In our model, the drive causes the NSS to gradually lose coherence over time. Under these long-time driving conditions, we show that the long-time behavior can be described by an effective open quantum system. We use this formalism to fully analyze the NSS, tracking how steady-state properties evolve with driving parameters and reaching expected thermal equilibrium under certain conditions. We compare our theoretical results to experimental data collected from a qubit in an open system, finding excellent agreement between the model and the experiments.

MongoDB is widely recognized for its document-oriented design, operational flexibility, and horizontal scalability, making the advancement of reliability mechanisms critical. Although the database marketed basic multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) as of version 3.0, it initially lacked strict transactional guarantees. This research validates that essential integrity properties—specifically isolation, durability, and atomicity—were absent across versions 2 through 3 of MongoDB. While earlier releases failed entirely on these fronts, 3.0 provided only partial support; notably, writes during uncommitted transactions could be queried by concurrent transactions, violating true isolation. Regarding durability, a power loss after a committed transaction could still result in the loss of unindexed writes within the same transaction, breaching atomicity and demonstrating that MongoDB has not offered true transactional integrity.

This paper presents a polynomial extension of the generalized Chebychev form of the Schrödinger-Courant equation. This version is characterized as a second-order differential equation with a singular term coupled with a polynomial potential of degree $2n$. Within the space of polynomials of degree at most $N$, the unique spectrum is found to be singular and lack defect, except specifically when $n$ is an integer; in those whole-number cases, the spectrum exhibits both defect and singularity. The eigenfunctions corresponding to this system are defined as Generalized Hermite Polynomials. The piecewise structure, lack of holomorphy, and basis properties of these functions are explored in detail, alongside a calculation of their monodromy. Finally, the article offers a series expansion for several well-known special functions, including Arcuus Tangent, Arcus Sine, various Jacobi elliptic functions, and Legendre Polynomials, expressed entirely without root terms.

Unrolling an adhesive tape produces a smooth rotational motion interspersed with sudden bursts of acoustic noise, a phenomenon known as crackling sound. The angles of rotation correspond linearly to the total path length uncovered; consequently, one can reconstruct the kinematic trajectory of unrolling with high precision by applying post-processing algorithms to the recorded sound of unrolling. Through this method, the study reveals that the seemingly chaotic acoustic pattern actually embodies concealed order. Indeed, the original temporal presentation obscures this hidden regularity, which becomes apparent when analyzing the data via phase space representations and symbolic dynamics.

In an extended Black-Scholean framework that incorporates liquidity costs, a novel analytical equation is derived to determine the value of options collateralized with a risky underlying asset and hedged dynamically. This main result also provides explicit formulas for the dynamic hedging strategy, related hedging risks, and the asset price path-dependent characteristics within the underlying process. As specific applications, the note utilizes its novel equation to derive static hedging strategies for both European and American puts, ultimately offering a clear definition for the marking-to-collateral process for these derivatives.

We present an observable, dynamic framework centered on skills-based, intergenerational mobility, addressing a significant challenge in designing public policies for education and employment. Unlike static models, this dynamic model reveals how varying the return on opportunities—such as education—can influence their utilization rates, entry thresholds, and overall impact on social流动性 (social mobility). Higher returns may enhance overall mobility by enabling broader access, yet they also risk widening the gap between high- and low-skilled individuals; conversely, lower supports wider mobility floors but might constrain overall upward movement. Calibrated against United States data, our model accurately reflects observed variations in educational attainment, mobility rates, and the distribution of career trajectories across different generations.

Brightness scans represent a fundamental technique in beam diagnostics, enabling the characterization of transverse electromagnetic beams—such as those in particle accelerators—by measuring the force exerted on a probe as it moves through dimensions perpendicular to the beam path. Historically, these scans have been limited to one direction at a time, relying on a brightness matrix derived from three force measurements at each scan scan to infer spatial distributions, including those of high-energy photons where direct detection at bright spots is challenging due to intensity levels. While existing models typically assume linear forces during positional scans, this work extends the standard approach by simulating both non-linear forces and scanned trajectories to better reflect operational realities, incorporating numerical methods that account for diffraction effects and space-charge interactions to enhance analytical precision.

This study examines a quantized and distributed optimization framework in which gradient information may be compromised by adversarial actors. The core challenge is to minimize a average cost function comprising both differentiable and nondifferentiable components, distributed across a connected, undirected graph with only local communication. Assuming that gradient data at specific nodes has been contaminated by arbitrary but limited-srength malicious attacks, this paper establishes an upper bound for the algorithm's convergence rate. Furthermore, it introduces a performance guarantee under the premise that gradient data at select nodes is accessible. Final simulations validate the theoretical results and demonstrate the method's efficacy in distinguishing between legitimate and adversarial nodes through performance guarantees.

Pyramid schemes represent a classic example of a zero-sum game, widely recognized for their appeal despite being illegal; these networks offer massive returns to early participants while solely utilizing contributions from later joiners. Traditionally, detecting and understanding their operational mechanics has been difficult due to the lack of accessible data and the inherent complexity of building such pyramids. This study focuses on Forsage (2020-2021), which appeared to be the most extensive financial pyramid scheme ever, operating through a smart contract. By analyzing Forsage's architecture, we demonstrate how its code fundamentally functions as a zero-sum mechanism with disproportionately growing costs. Finally, we outline the necessary indicators for identifying similar schemes implemented as smart contracts.

Disease transmission represents one of humanity's most significant challenges in the 21st century, with biological motions—including those of pathogens, vectors, and larger organisms—playing a pivotal role. This motion often influences the progression of illnesses alongside the organisms themselves. Recognizing and understanding these patterns is crucial for developing effective detection and mitigation strategies against various diseases. In this paper, we detail the protocols used to construct the database, describe the motion detection methods developed during the project, and showcase its utility by analyzing the locomotion patterns of flies, frogs, and worms within natural settings.

These findings represent a substantial improvement in performance, opening avenues for real-time performance in rendering and scientific modeling.

This study models and simulates the interaction between a one-legged hopper with a single degree of freedom (DOF) and yield-based terrain, utilizing both physical experiments and computational methods to establish a predictive model for terrain yield. The proposed simulation framework integrates three core components: an event-driven dynamics solver, a yield terrain model, and a plasticity solver tailored specifically to Hoppe's stick-slip conditions. By introducing a novel energy release function that aligns with Hoppe's friction framework, this solver enhances standard terrain yield models, which typically rely on critical velocity or force thresholds but lack the capacity to represent local deformations caused by stick-slip dynamics. Hoppe's original physical laws were applied to simulate dry friction between a deformable tip and soil; while effective for that context, the approach extends to other soil deformation modes like shear failure or dilation. One legged hopper controllers designed for rigid environments were tested against the new simulated yielding environment, revealing that classical control strategies fail under soft conditions due to energy loss from deformation and altered slip velocities. In the Weyl-Wigner framework of quantum mechanics, operators are mapped according to canonical transformation rules that mirror the classical Poisson bracket structure. By substituting the von Neumann equation and local canonical equilibrium density matrix with their respective Weyl-Wigner representations, we derive the quantized Hamilton-Liouville equation and a corresponding integral constraint. Together, these formulations define the Weyl-Wigner generalized canonical equilibrium conditions. Notably, this framework allows for the derivation of the Weyl-Wigner expressions for the local canonical quantum equilibrium density operator from the classical version. Furthermore, we identify the Weyl-Wigner forms of two additional long-standing conditions: the Thomas-Fermi model and the local mean-field approximation (encompassing Hartree and Hartree-ree conditions). Results recently presented by the lead author regarding local canonical conditions in the Wick symbol representation are also reconciled within this framework.

The concept of negative absolute temperature finds its footing in nuclear spin ensembles and other systems exhibiting an inverted population, coexisting alongside temperatures ranging from zero to infinity and sharing the same thermal units. Despite appearing counterintuitive, this notion is well-established within statistical mechanics and experimental practice. We argue for reviving interest in negative temperature research, as these systems display exceptionally short coupling with conventional, positive-temperature substances, thereby actually attaining even more extreme, effective temperatures than theoretically noted. This characteristic profoundly impacts the potential applications of technologies such as lasers, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and NMR-based imaging (MRI). The article explores the implications of this fact across various domains, including astrophysics, thermodynamics, and both classical and quantum mechanics, as well as electromagnetism, optics, and condensed matter science. We also examine relevant elementary mathematical frameworks like differential equations, sequences, and polynomials, along with foundational physical theories such as Einstein's Special Relativity and Newton's Laws of Motion, and their broader applications. This wide-ranging investigation holds significant educational value for students at high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels.

Vector data represents geometric objects like points, lines, and surfaces along with their inherent non-linear attributes. Although software exists to 2D/3D-display this geometry paired with some attributes, current tools fall short in handling high-dimensional datasets or offering intuitive interactive analysis of every object and its complete attribute set. We introduce *ViDaExpert*, a solution designed to facilitate the analysis of every-dimensional object data by integrating a traditional 3D viewer with an intelligent table-based inspector. After evaluating *ViDaExpert* with professional 3Data Li users, feedback confirmed that enhancing dimensionality analysis through such an interface is highly beneficial, as it enables tasks and insights previously unachievable.
